p: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were two feasts side by side. By Jesus' day people used either name for both.
b: In the Law, Passover is the lamb killed on the fourteenth of the month Nisan, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread is the seven days that follow (Leviticus 23:5–6). In practice the eight days ran together, and Josephus too speaks of the feast of unleavened bread "which we call Passover" (Jewish Antiquities 14.21). Luke explains the name, as he often does for readers who were not Jews. Passover remembered the night God brought Israel out of Egypt, so it was a feast of freedom, and Jerusalem filled with pilgrims. That is why the authorities feared the crowds (22:2).
r: Exodus 12:1–20; Leviticus 23:5–8; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Mark 14:1; Matthew 26:2; John 11:55

a: because the people made them afraid
p: In Luke the people are on Jesus' side almost to the end. The leaders fear them.
b: Luke keeps "the people" (laos) apart from their rulers. The people hang on Jesus' words in the temple (19:48; 21:38), and the leaders cannot act openly because of them (20:19; 22:2, 6). Only at 23:13–23 does a crowd join the cry for crucifixion, and afterward the people go home beating their chests (23:48). This matters for how the passion has been read: Luke does not paint "the Jews" as one block against Jesus. See the note at 23:25.

p: After the testing in the wilderness the devil left Jesus alone "until his next chance." Luke says that time has come.
b: At the end of the testing the devil "left him alone until his next chance" (4:13). Luke has not mentioned him acting directly against Jesus since; now he enters Judas, and Jesus speaks of the "authority of darkness" (22:53). John says the same thing in other words (John 13:2, 27). Luke does not use Satan to excuse Judas: Judas goes off and makes the deal himself (22:4–6), and Jesus says "woe to that man" (22:22). Readers have weighed the two sides ever since. Some stress that evil works through human choices; others, that the passion is a battle with a power greater than any one person, and that God's plan stands over both (Acts 2:23).

a: who was counted among the Twelve
p: Luke stresses that Judas was one of the inner circle. Peter will say the same in Acts 1:17.
b: The Greek is literally "being of the number of the Twelve." In Acts, Peter says of Judas that "He was counted as one of us, and he got his allotted share in this service" (Acts 1:17), and the apostles then choose Matthias so that the Twelve are whole again (Acts 1:26). The betrayal comes from inside the circle, as the psalm foresaw (Psalm 41:9). See the note at 22:21.

p: Officers of the temple guard, priests in charge of the Levites who policed the temple courts.
b: The Greek stratēgoi are "commanders." In 22:52 Luke calls them "commanders of the temple," and in Acts the commander of the temple arrests the apostles (Acts 4:1; 5:24–26). Josephus names such an officer (Jewish Antiquities 20.131). Their men were Levites, not Roman soldiers, which fits an arrest planned by the temple leadership. Only Luke brings these officers into Judas' bargain.

p: Luke, like Mark, does not name a sum. Matthew says thirty silver coins, the price in Zechariah 11.
b: Argyrion means silver, and so money. Mark 14:11 also leaves the amount unnamed. Matthew 26:15 says the priests weighed out thirty silver coins, and Matthew later ties the sum to Zechariah 11:12–13. In Acts, Luke says Judas came to own a piece of land "with the pay he got for doing wrong" (Acts 1:18).

a: the day when they were required to sacrifice the Passover lamb
p: On the afternoon of Nisan 14 the lambs were killed at the temple, to be eaten that night.
b: The Law says to slaughter the lamb "between the two evenings" (Exodus 12:6), which by Jesus' time meant the afternoon. Each household or group brought its lamb to the temple, where priests caught the blood and splashed it on the altar. Josephus says a count once made under Nero came to more than 250,000 victims at one Passover (Jewish War 6.9.3); the number is probably inflated, but the scale was huge. Luke, like Mark and Matthew, treats the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John places the crucifixion on the day the lambs were killed (John 19:14). The deep dive at Matthew 26 sets out the ways scholars handle this.
r: Exodus 12:6; Deuteronomy 16:5–6; Mark 14:12; Matthew 26:17; John 18:28; John 19:14

p: Only Luke names the two who prepared the meal. They will work as a pair in Acts.
b: Mark says only "two of his disciples" (Mark 14:13). Luke names Peter and John, and in Acts the same two go up to the temple to pray, heal a lame man, stand trial together and go to Samaria (Acts 3:1; 4:13, 19; 8:14). Luke likes to show the leaders of the church learning to serve before they lead (22:26–27).

a: a man carrying a clay jar of water
p: Carrying water was usually women's work, so the man would stand out. Was it arranged, or foreknown?
b: In the villages of Israel women usually fetched water in jars, as at Genesis 24:11 and John 4:7, and men carried skins. A man with a jar would be easy to spot. Arranged: many readers think Jesus had agreed on this with a friend in the city, keeping the place secret so that Judas could not betray him before the meal. Foreknown: others read it, like the colt in 19:30–34, as Jesus' prophetic knowledge, the way Samuel told Saul exactly whom he would meet (1 Samuel 10:2–7). Luke tells it in nearly the same words as the colt story, which suggests he wants the two scenes read together.

t: The same room as at Bethlehem
p: Luke uses katalyma only twice: for the place with no room at Jesus' birth, and for the room of the Last Supper.
b: At Jesus' birth there was "no space for them in the guest room" (2:7), using katalyma, the word the old translations render "inn." Here the same word plainly means a guest room in a private house, and that is why many scholars, Kenneth Bailey among them, think 2:7 means a crowded guest room too, not a hotel. The Gospel that began with no room for the newborn Jesus ends with Jesus as host in a guest room, giving himself to his friends. Mark 14:14 has "my" room (to katalyma mou), which Mark's Plain renders "the room for me to stay"; Luke has no "my," and the Plain keeps "guest room" so the link with 2:7 shows.

a: he lay down at the table
p: At a Passover meal everyone reclined on couches, as free people did. The Mishnah says even the poorest must recline.
b: Ordinary meals were often eaten sitting, but feasts were eaten reclining on cushions or couches, leaning on the left elbow. The Mishnah says that on Passover night "even the poorest in Israel must not eat until he reclines" (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1), because reclining was the posture of free people, and the feast celebrates freedom from slavery. The first Passover in Egypt was eaten standing, dressed for travel (Exodus 12:11). Luke calls the Twelve "the apostles" here, the title they will carry in Acts.

p: A Hebrew-style doubling that makes the desire strong. The Greek Old Testament uses the same phrase in Genesis 31:30.
b: The Greek epithymia epethymēsa repeats the word: "with desire I desired." This copies a Hebrew way of strengthening a verb, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same phrase where Laban says Jacob longed to go home (Genesis 31:30). Luke writes much of his Gospel in this Bible-like Greek. The usual meaning of epithymia is "desire," often bad desire ("lust"), but here it is Jesus' deep wish to share this meal before he suffers.

a: comes to its fulfillment in the kingdom of God
p: Jesus treats the Passover as a picture of something still to come: the feast of God's kingdom.
b: Passover looked back to the rescue from Egypt, but Jews also hoped for a final rescue on Passover night, and the prophets pictured God's future as a banquet: "the LORD of Armies will spread a feast for all the peoples" (Isaiah 25:6). Jesus has spoken of people coming from east and west to recline in the kingdom of God (13:29) and of the one who will eat bread there (14:15). He now says the Passover finds its meaning there. Christians have heard in this the hope that the Lord's Supper looks toward, "until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26).

p: Only Luke has a cup before the bread as well as after it. Readers have explained it in several ways.
b: Luke's longer text has a cup at 22:17 and another "when the meal was over" (22:20). The Passover cups: the Passover meal had four cups of wine (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1–7), so many think the first cup here is an early cup of the meal and the second is the cup after supper, which Paul calls "the cup of blessing" (1 Corinthians 10:16). Two sources: others think Luke joined a farewell saying about not drinking again (22:15–18) to the words over bread and cup that the churches used (22:19–20), which match Paul's (1 Corinthians 11:23–25). The shorter text: in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts there is only one cup, before the bread; see the variant at 22:19 and the deep dive on this chapter page.

p: Jewish blessings over wine thank God "who creates the fruit of the vine." Jesus' saying uses the same phrase.
b: Before drinking wine, Jews said a blessing to God "who creates the fruit of the vine" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1), and the phrase is still said over the cup at a Seder and at the Sabbath meal. Mark and Matthew place this saying after the cup of the covenant; Luke places it before the bread, as a farewell: Jesus will not drink again until the kingdom has come.

p: Luke's words over the bread and cup are closest to Paul's in 1 Corinthians 11, the earliest written account.
b: Mark and Matthew say Jesus "said the blessing" over the bread (eulogēsas); Luke says he "gave thanks" (eucharistēsas), the word that gives "Eucharist," and so does Paul. Luke and Paul also share "which is (being) given for you," "Do this to remember me," "after supper" and "the new covenant in my blood" (1 Corinthians 11:23–25). Paul wrote about AD 54 and says he passed on what he had received. So Luke seems to follow a form of the words used in Paul's churches, while Mark and Matthew follow another.

p: Anamnēsis is a remembering that makes the past present. Churches differ on what more it means.
b: "For my remembrance" (eis tēn emēn anamnēsin) uses the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the memorial portion of an offering and for remembrance before God (Leviticus 24:7; Numbers 10:10). Passover itself was a "day of remembrance" (Exodus 12:14), when each generation told the story as its own. Memorial: many Protestants read the words as a command to recall Christ's death. Making present: Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican and Lutheran teachers say that in the liturgy the one sacrifice of the cross is made present, not repeated. God's remembering: Joachim Jeremias argued that the phrase asks God to remember the Messiah, but few have followed him. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter page.
orig: εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν (eis tēn emēn anamnēsin)

p: Jeremiah promised "a new covenant." Mark and Matthew say "my blood of the covenant," recalling Sinai.
b: Jeremiah wrote: "I will cut a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" (Jeremiah 31:31), a covenant written on hearts, with sins forgiven. At Sinai Moses splashed blood on the people and said, "Here is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you" (Exodus 24:8). Mark and Matthew echo Sinai; Luke and Paul name Jeremiah's "new covenant" (1 Corinthians 11:25). The phrase gave the Christian Scriptures their later name, "New Testament," since Latin testamentum rendered "covenant."
r: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Exodus 24:8; Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 8:8–13

a: It is being poured out for you
p: In Greek, "poured out" agrees with "cup," not with "blood." Scholars use this in the debate over these verses.
b: The participle to ... ekchynnomenon is in the case of "the cup," not of "my blood," so the Greek says, strictly, that the cup is being poured out. Mark 14:24 has the participle agree with "blood." Some scholars, following Westcott and Hort, took the clumsy grammar as a sign that 22:19b–20 were stitched in from Paul and Mark; others answer that a copyist adding the words would have smoothed them, so the roughness is a mark of age. The Plain keeps the meaning without forcing the grammar. See the variant at 22:19.
orig: τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυννόμενον (to hyper hymōn ekchynnomenon)

a: has his hand here with mine on the table
p: Luke puts the warning after the bread and cup, so Judas has shared them. A psalm tells of a friend who ate one's bread.
b: In Mark and Matthew Jesus speaks of the betrayer before the bread and cup; in Luke after them, so that the betrayer has eaten the same meal. Psalm 41 laments a friend "who ate my bread" and "has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9), and John quotes it of Judas (John 13:18). In the ancient world, sharing a table bound people as friends, which made betrayal by a table companion especially shameful.

a: as it has been marked out
p: Luke's verb means "determined, fixed in advance." He uses it for God's plan in Acts, beside human responsibility.
b: Mark says "as it stands written about him" (Mark 14:21). Luke says kata to hōrismenon, "according to what has been fixed." In Acts the same verb describes Jesus handed over "by the plan God had fixed" (Acts 2:23) and appointed judge (Acts 10:42; 17:31). In the same breath Jesus pronounces woe on the betrayer. Luke holds the two together without explaining how: God's purpose stands, and the human act is still guilty.

p: Luke moves the dispute about greatness to the Last Supper, making 22:24–38 a farewell speech.
b: Mark and Matthew place a similar dispute on the road to Jerusalem (Mark 10:41–45; Matthew 20:24–28). Luke sets it at the table, after the bread and cup, and follows it with a kingdom bequeathed (22:29), a prediction about Peter (22:31–34) and a warning about hard times (22:35–38). Ancient readers knew this shape: a great man's last words at a final meal, with warnings and charges to his heirs, as in Jacob's blessings (Genesis 49), Moses' farewell (Deuteronomy 31–33), the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, John 13–17 and Paul at Miletus (Acts 20:17–38).

p: Hellenistic kings and Roman rulers took the title Euergetēs, "Benefactor," for gifts that bound subjects to them.
b: Two Ptolemies of Egypt were called Euergetes, and inscriptions across the Greek East honor kings, governors and rich citizens as "benefactors" for buildings, grain and games. The gifts were real, and so was the obligation they created: the giver received honor and loyalty. Jesus does not deny that rulers give; he says his followers must not use giving to rule. Frederick Danker gathered the inscriptions in Benefactor (1982).

a: like the one who waits on tables
p: Ho diakonōn, "the one serving," is the waiter at a meal. The word family gives "deacon."
b: In a house the one who "served" brought the food while others lay at the table. Jesus asks the obvious question, who is greater, and then turns the answer upside down: "I, in your company, am like the one who waits on tables." John tells the same lesson as an act, when Jesus washes the disciples' feet (John 13:4–15). Mark 10:45 adds that the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom. In Acts the apostles choose seven to "serve tables" (Acts 6:2), and later the church called such servants deacons.

p: Peirasmoi are tests or trials. Luke sees Jesus' whole ministry as a time of testing since the wilderness.
b: The same word family runs through Luke: the devil tested Jesus (4:2, 13), and Jesus tells the disciples to pray not to come into testing (22:40, 46; compare 11:4). Here he thanks them for standing by him through it all, just before they fail him. Luke's tone toward the Twelve is gentler than Mark's: he praises their loyalty before their flight, and he never says they ran away (compare Mark 14:50).

a: I am making over to you a kingdom
p: Diatithemai is the root of diathēkē, "covenant" or "will": Jesus hands on a kingdom as by a last will.
b: Just after naming "the new covenant" (diathēkē, 22:20), Jesus uses the verb from the same root: "I covenant to you," or "I bequeath to you, as my Father bequeathed to me, a kingdom." The word was used for drawing up a will (Hebrews 9:16–17 plays on both senses). At a farewell meal, the dying master leaves his heirs not money but a share in his rule, and a place at his table.

a: judge the twelve tribes of Israel
p: Matthew 19:28 has the same promise. The Twelve stand for Israel renewed. "Judge" may mean "rule."
b: Matthew has it in another setting: "you too will sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28). Luke says "on thrones," without "twelve," perhaps because Judas is present. The number twelve shows that Jesus was gathering a renewed Israel; in Acts the apostles fill Judas' place before Pentecost (Acts 1:26), and the disciples ask about the kingdom for Israel (Acts 1:6). To judge may mean to condemn, but in the Old Testament "judges" were leaders who ruled and rescued, and many take the promise in that sense. Jewish hope expected the twelve tribes to be gathered again (Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28).
r: Matthew 19:28; Acts 1:6; Acts 1:26; Daniel 7:9–10; Daniel 7:22; Revelation 21:12–14; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28

p: Satan wants all the disciples (Greek plural). Jesus has prayed for Simon (singular). English "you" hides the shift.
b: In 22:31 "you" is plural, hymas: Satan has asked for all of them. In 22:32 it is singular, sou: Jesus has prayed for Simon, so that he can strengthen the rest. The scene recalls Job, where the accuser asks God for leave to test a righteous man (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6), and Amos 9:9, where God shakes Israel as in a sieve. Sifting shakes grain so that the chaff and dirt fall away; the image is of a hard test, not of destruction. Jesus calls him "Simon," his old name, as if Peter, "rock," is not yet what he will be.

a: that your faith would not fail
p: Jesus prays not that Peter won't fall, but that his faith won't die out. Catholic teaching also reads it of the popes.
b: Peter will deny Jesus three times that night, yet his faith will not "fail" (eklipē, "give out," the verb Luke uses of the sun at 23:45). The First Vatican Council cited this verse in teaching that the faith of Peter's see would not fail (Pastor Aeternus 4). Orthodox and Protestant readers take the promise as personal to Peter, kept when he turned back after his denial. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter page, and the card on Peter at Matthew 16:18.

p: Epistrephō is the Bible's word for turning back to God. Peter's restoring is foretold before his fall.
b: The verb means to turn around, and in Acts it describes repentance: "repent and turn around" (Acts 3:19). Jesus speaks as if the fall is certain and the return is certain too. Luke never narrates Peter's restoring, but the risen Lord appears to him first (24:34), and in Acts Peter stands up among the brothers and leads them (Acts 1:15; 2:14). John tells the restoring in a scene by the lake (John 21:15–19).

p: Mark has "before a rooster crows twice"; Luke and Matthew simply "before a rooster crows."
b: All four Gospels have the prediction (Mark 14:30; Matthew 26:34; John 13:38). Luke places it at the table, as John does; Mark and Matthew place it on the way to the Mount of Olives. In Luke Jesus calls him "Peter" for the only time in the Gospel, just as he predicts the denial; the name means "rock."

a: without a money purse, a bag or sandals
t: The old rules and the new
p: Jesus recalls the mission orders of 9:3 and 10:4. Then they lacked nothing; now times will be hostile.
b: When Jesus sent out the Twelve and then the seventy(-two), he told them to take nothing for the road and depend on the hospitality of those who welcomed them (9:3–5; 10:4–7). Jesus now reverses those orders. The point is that the welcome is over: as he is about to be treated like an outlaw (22:37), his followers will face rejection too, and must be ready to fend for themselves.

p: One of Jesus' hardest sayings. Most readers take it as a picture of coming danger; some, literally.
b: A figure of speech: the saying is a vivid way of saying "hard times are coming; be ready for conflict." The disciples take it literally and produce two swords, and Jesus ends the talk (22:38) and later stops their use of the sword (22:51). Calvin and most modern commentators read it this way. Fulfilling Scripture: the swords make the group look like outlaws, so that Jesus is "counted with the lawless" (22:37). Self-defense: some read it as allowing travelers to carry arms against robbers, but not to defend the gospel by force. Revolution: S. G. F. Brandon (1967) argued that Jesus was close to the Zealots; most scholars reject that reading. See the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter page.

a: 'And he was counted with the lawless.'
p: The only place in the Gospels where Jesus quotes Isaiah 53. It comes true when he is crucified between criminals.
b: The Hebrew of Isaiah 53:12 says the servant "was counted with the rebels" (Isaiah 53:12), and the Greek Old Testament says "with the lawless." Luke's wording is close to the Greek. This is the only direct quotation of Isaiah's suffering servant song by Jesus in the Gospels, though the song lies behind many sayings (Mark 10:45; Acts 8:32–35). Luke shows it fulfilled: Jesus is arrested like a bandit (22:52) and crucified with two criminals (23:32–33).

p: Is Jesus saying two swords will do, or cutting off a conversation the disciples have misunderstood?
b: Hikanon estin can mean "that is sufficient." Two are enough for the purpose of 22:37, to be counted among outlaws, but far too few to fight. Enough of this!: many take it as a weary end to a misunderstanding, as God says to Moses, "That is enough from you!" (Deuteronomy 3:26), using a related word in the Greek Old Testament. In the Middle Ages the verse was read as an allegory of "two swords," spiritual and worldly power, both belonging to the church (Pope Boniface VIII, Unam Sanctam, 1302). No church today rests its teaching on that reading.

p: Jesus had spent his nights on the Mount of Olives (21:37). Judas knew where to find him.
b: Luke says Jesus taught in the temple by day and spent the nights on the Mount of Olives, as it is called (21:37). Luke does not use the name Gethsemane, "oil press" (Mark 14:32), but says only "the place." John says Judas knew the place because Jesus often met there with his disciples (John 18:2). Pilgrims at Passover often camped outside the crowded city.

a: Pray not to come into testing
p: Jesus' words echo the Lord's Prayer: "do not bring us into testing." They frame the scene, at 22:40 and 22:46.
b: Luke opens and closes the scene with the same charge (22:40, 46), and in between Jesus himself prays. The phrase recalls the last line of the prayer he taught them (11:4; Matthew 6:13). The "testing" is the hour when faith is put under strain, as Peter's will be within hours.

p: Jews usually prayed standing. Kneeling marked urgent prayer. Mark says he fell to the ground.
b: In the temple people prayed standing (18:11, 13). Kneeling appears in times of special need or deep humility: Solomon at the dedication (1 Kings 8:54), Daniel (Daniel 6:10), Stephen as he dies (Acts 7:60), Peter beside Tabitha (Acts 9:40), Paul with the elders (Acts 20:36; 21:5). Mark and Matthew say Jesus fell on the ground or on his face. Luke's wording becomes the pattern for Christian prayer in Acts.
r: 1 Kings 8:54; Daniel 6:10; Acts 7:60; Acts 9:40; Acts 20:36; Mark 14:35; Matthew 26:39

a: make this cup pass me by
p: In the prophets the cup is God's anger, which the nations must drink. Jesus asks whether it can pass him by.
b: Isaiah says Jerusalem drank "the cup of his fury" from the LORD's hand (Isaiah 51:17), and Jeremiah is told to make the nations drink the cup of the wine of God's anger (Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus had asked James and John whether they could drink the cup he drinks (Mark 10:38). Wrath: many readers hold that Jesus faces the judgment due to others. Suffering: others take the cup more simply as the suffering and death before him. Both readings let the prayer show Jesus' human dread and his obedience, which the church later defended against those who said Jesus had no human will (the Third Council of Constantinople, 681).
r: Isaiah 51:17; Isaiah 51:22; Jeremiah 25:15–16; Psalm 75:8; Mark 10:38–39; Mark 14:36; Hebrews 5:7–8

p: Like Elijah under the broom tree, Jesus is strengthened by an angel for what lies ahead.
b: When Elijah lay exhausted in the wilderness, an angel touched him and gave him food: "You have too far to go" (1 Kings 19:7). Daniel too is strengthened by a heavenly figure (Daniel 10:18–19). Luke's verb is ōphthē, "appeared," the word used when the risen Lord "has appeared to Simon" (24:34). The angel does not take the cup away; he gives strength to drink it. These verses are missing from many early manuscripts; see the variant on this verse and the deep dive on this chapter page.

p: Agōnia is the tension of an athlete before a contest. It gives English "agony."
b: The word comes from agōn, a contest or race. Greek writers used agōnia for the strain and anxiety of someone about to fight. Luke pictures Jesus as a contender gathering himself for the struggle, and praying "harder still" (ektenesteron, "more earnestly, more stretched out"), a word Luke uses for the church's prayer for Peter in prison (Acts 12:5).

p: Luke says "like" drops of blood. Some think he means real bloody sweat, a rare condition doctors describe.
b: The Greek hōsei thromboi haimatos means "as if clots of blood." A comparison: many read it as a picture of heavy sweat falling in thick drops, the way blood drips from a wound. Bloody sweat: others point to hematidrosis, a rare condition reported in modern medical writing, in which blood vessels near the sweat glands break under extreme stress; William Edwards and colleagues mention it in their study of Jesus' death (1986). Older writers argued that Luke, "the dear doctor" of Colossians 4:14, used medical language here (Hobart, 1882), but Henry Cadbury showed that such words were common among educated writers, so the verse cannot prove Luke was a physician.

p: In Mark Jesus finds them asleep three times. Luke tells it once, and explains: they slept from grief.
b: Mark has three returns and three rebukes (Mark 14:37–41). Luke has one, and gives a reason that softens it: "from grief" (apo tēs lypēs). This fits Luke's gentler picture of the Twelve (see the note at 22:28). Some readers see deep sorrow causing exhaustion; others, a sleep of escape. Either way Jesus' charge is the same: get up and pray.

a: He came up close to Jesus to kiss him
p: Mark and Matthew say Judas kissed Jesus. Luke says only that he came to do it, and Jesus speaks first.
b: A kiss was the usual greeting of a disciple to a teacher. Mark 14:44–45 and Matthew 26:48–49 make it the agreed signal. Luke does not mention the signal, and Jesus' question (22:48) seems to come before the kiss, so that Jesus stays in control of the scene. Proverbs says "kisses from someone who hates you come thick and fast" (Proverbs 27:6). The question "with a kiss you hand over the Son of Man?" puts the gesture of friendship and the act of betrayal side by side.

a: are we to strike with the sword?
p: Only Luke has the disciples ask first. One strikes before Jesus answers.
b: The disciples' question shows they have taken 22:36–38 literally. Luke alone includes the question, and the swords they had shown Jesus now come into play. The Greek uses ei to introduce a direct question, a Septuagint habit.
orig: εἰ πατάξομεν ἐν μαχαίρῃ; (ei pataxomen en machairē?)

a: Touching the ear, he healed him
p: Only Luke tells that Jesus healed the slave's ear. It is his last miracle before the cross, done for an enemy.
b: All four Gospels tell of the cut ear, and John names the slave, Malchus, and the swordsman, Peter (John 18:10). Only Luke says Jesus touched the ear and healed it. Jesus had taught, "keep loving your enemies. Treat well the people who hate you" (6:27), and here he does it in the hour of his arrest. Readers have seen in the act both mercy and a refusal of armed defense (see the card on this chapter page).

p: The Greek is brief and unclear: "Allow up to this." To whom, and what?
b: Eate heōs toutou literally means "Allow until this." To the disciples: "Stop! No more of this." Most translations read it so. To the arresting party: "Let me do this much," asking to touch and heal the wounded man. To the disciples, of the arrest: "Let them go on; let it happen," since this is the hour. The words that follow, the healing, fit any of them.

a: the chief priests, the commanders of the temple and the elders
p: Only Luke has the chief priests themselves at the arrest. Mark says the crowd came from them.
b: In Mark and Matthew the crowd is sent by the chief priests and elders. In John a cohort of soldiers and temple police come (John 18:3, 12). Luke puts the leaders at the scene, so that Jesus can speak to them face to face: they had every chance to arrest him in the temple by day.

p: Night, the arrest and Satan's work come together. Paul uses the very phrase: "the authority of darkness."
b: Luke has shown Satan entering Judas (22:3) and seeking to sift the disciples (22:31). The arrest happens at night, and when Jesus dies darkness covers the land (23:44–45). Colossians 1:13 uses the same Greek phrase, saying God "rescued us from the authority of darkness" and moved us into his Son's kingdom; Paul's commission in Acts is to help people "turn back from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God" (Acts 26:18). The hour belongs to darkness, but only for an hour.
orig: ἡ ἐξουσία τοῦ σκότους (hē exousia tou skotous)

p: Luke does not name the high priest here. Caiaphas held the office, but his father-in-law Annas was still powerful.
b: Luke named "the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas" at 3:2. Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36 (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.35, 95); Annas had held the office earlier and five of his sons held it later. John says Jesus was taken first to Annas (John 18:13). In 1990 a family tomb in Jerusalem yielded an ornate ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas," probably the high priest's. Large priestly houses excavated in the Upper City show courtyards like the one in this scene.

a: in the center of the courtyard
p: Luke tells all three denials during the night, and the hearing before the council in the morning.
b: Mark sandwiches the night trial between the start and end of Peter's denials (Mark 14:53–72). Luke tells the story in a straight line: the denials and the mockery by night (22:54–65), the council at daybreak (22:66–71). Many think Luke has tidied Mark's account; others think Luke had his own source, which fits a single morning session of the council, the time when a court could lawfully meet (compare Mark 15:1).

a: He is a Galilean, after all
p: Matthew says Peter's speech gave him away. Galileans' Aramaic sounded different to Judeans.
b: Matthew 26:73 explains: "The way you talk shows it." Galileans were known for dropping or blurring some sounds, and the Babylonian Talmud has stories mocking Galileans who could not keep certain sounds apart (Eruvin 53b). Peter, a fisherman from the lake, would have sounded like a northerner.

a: The Lord turned around and fixed his eyes on Peter
p: Only Luke tells of the look. It suggests Jesus was in the courtyard during the denials.
b: Luke alone says the Lord turned and looked at Peter. In Luke's order the hearing comes later, at daybreak, so Jesus is still being held in or near the courtyard while Peter denies him. The verb emblepō means to look straight at someone, as Jesus looked at the rich ruler (Mark 10:21) and at those who questioned him (20:17). Luke calls him "the Lord" twice in this verse: the one Peter denies is Peter's Lord, and his word comes true.

a: Be a prophet! Who struck you?
p: The guards mock Jesus as a false prophet just after his prophecy about Peter came true.
b: Blindfolding a prisoner and asking him to guess who hit him was a cruel game. The irony is plain to Luke's readers: a few lines earlier Jesus' word to Peter was fulfilled to the letter (22:61). Luke presents Jesus as a prophet throughout (4:24; 7:16; 13:33; 24:19), and a prophet rejected in Jerusalem (13:33–34).

p: The Greek is "blaspheming." In Mark the council charges Jesus with blasphemy; in Luke the guards blaspheme him.
b: Blasphēmeō means to slander or speak abusively, against God or against people. Mark has the high priest say "You heard the blasphemy" (Mark 14:64). Luke never calls Jesus' words blasphemy; instead the guards "blaspheme" him. Luke uses the same verb for the criminal who insults Jesus on the cross (23:39). The Plain says "reviling" both times so that readers can see the link.

p: Presbyterion, a body of elders, is the word the church later used for its own elders.
b: Luke calls the council to presbyterion tou laou, "the eldership of the people," and then their synedrion, the Sanhedrin, which may mean the council or the room where it met. Paul uses presbyterion of the same council in Acts 22:5, and 1 Timothy 4:14 uses it for a church's body of elders, the source of English "presbytery." On the makeup of the Sanhedrin, see the note at Mark 14:55 and the topic page.
orig: τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τοῦ λαοῦ (to presbyterion tou laou)

a: If I tell you, you will never believe it
p: Jesus' answer echoes Jeremiah's words to King Zedekiah, in the Greek Old Testament.
b: When Zedekiah questioned Jeremiah in secret, the prophet answered that if he told the king, the king would put him to death, and if he gave advice, the king would not listen (Jeremiah 38:15; the Greek Old Testament numbers the chapter 45). Jesus' double "if" has the same shape. Luke splits the council's question in two, asking first whether he is the Messiah (22:67) and then whether he is the Son of God (22:70).

a: the right hand of God's Power
p: Luke leaves out "you will see ... coming with the clouds." He stresses that Jesus will reign from now on.
b: Mark has Jesus say the council "will see the Son of Man sitting at the Power's right hand and coming with the clouds" (Mark 14:62), joining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. Luke has neither "you will see" nor the clouds, and he begins "from this time on." The church's present: many think Luke stresses Jesus' enthronement at the resurrection and ascension, which Stephen sees in Acts 7:56. The council's future: others note that the leaders will not see a coming in their lifetime, a change some connect with the delay of the end. "God's Power" is a reverent way of saying "God." Luke keeps Mark's "sitting" (estai ... kathēmenos, "will be sitting"): a lasting state, not a single act.
r: Psalm 110:1; Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 14:62; Matthew 26:64; Acts 2:33–35; Acts 7:55–56

a: It is you who say that I am
p: The answer can be heard as "Yes, as you say" or as "That is your way of putting it." The council takes it as yes.
b: The Greek hymeis legete hoti egō eimi means "You say that I am." A yes: the council treats it as a confession (22:71), and many take it as a guarded yes, putting the words back into the questioners' mouths. A qualified answer: others hear Jesus refusing their terms while not denying the claim. Mark has the plain "I am" (Mark 14:62). Luke saves "Son of God" for the second question, so that the title on which the hearing turns is the one the angel announced at the start (1:35).
orig: Ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι (Hymeis legete hoti egō eimi)

a: We ourselves have heard it straight from his mouth
p: Luke's hearing has no false witnesses, no charge of blasphemy and no death sentence. They take him to Pilate.
b: Mark and Matthew report false witnesses, the temple saying, a charge of blasphemy and a vote for death (Mark 14:55–64). Luke has none of these; the false witnesses and the temple saying appear in Acts at Stephen's trial (Acts 6:13–14). Luke's council acts more like a body preparing a case for Rome, which matches the charges they bring to Pilate (23:2). Scholars debate whether Luke had a separate source or reshaped Mark.

p: The Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. Only he could order a crucifixion.
b: Pilate governed Judea for the emperor Tiberius; a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names him "prefect of Judea." He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at festivals, with troops, to keep order. Philo quotes a letter that charges him with bribery, insults and executions without trial (On the Embassy to Gaius 302), and Josephus tells of riots he provoked (Jewish Antiquities 18.55–62). Luke has already mentioned his killing of Galileans at the altar (13:1). The Jewish authorities could not lawfully carry out a death sentence themselves (John 18:31), so they brought Jesus to him.

p: In the Greek Old Testament, Ahab calls Elijah the one who "perverts Israel," with the same verb.
b: Diastrephō means to twist, pervert, lead astray. When Ahab met Elijah he said, "So it's you, the one who brings trouble on Israel!" (1 Kings 18:17), and the Greek Old Testament uses this same verb there. Luke's readers who knew their Greek Bible would hear the charge as one more case of a prophet accused by the powerful. The three charges are built for a Roman ear: unrest, refusing tax, and a rival king.

a: He hinders people from paying taxes to Caesar
p: Luke's readers know the charge is false: Jesus had said, "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" (20:25).
b: The leaders had tried to trap Jesus with the question of tax (20:20–26), hoping to hand him over to the governor. He had answered in a way they could not use. Here they simply say the opposite. Luke tells his readers, who lived under Rome, that the charge of sedition against Jesus and his movement was untrue, a theme he carries into Acts (Acts 17:6–7; 24:5; 25:8).

p: Without the article, "Messiah, a king" translates a Jewish title into a political one for a Roman judge.
b: The Greek has christon basilea with no article: "Christ, a king." To Pilate, "Christ" would mean nothing; "king" would mean rebellion against Caesar. So Pilate's first question is "So you are the King of the Jews?" (23:3). Luke shows how the Jewish hope of an anointed son of David could be turned into a charge of treason.

a: You are the one saying it
p: The same answer as in Mark 15:2. Pilate does not treat it as a confession of guilt.
b: The Greek sy legeis, "you say," neither denies nor fully accepts the title in Pilate's sense. In Luke, Pilate goes straight on to declare Jesus innocent (23:4), which suggests he heard no claim to be a rebel king. John expands the exchange: "My kingdom does not come from this world" (John 18:36).

a: I find nothing to charge this man with
p: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times (23:4, 14, 22). Herod, a criminal and a centurion agree.
b: Luke builds a chain of witnesses: Pilate three times (23:4, 14–15, 22), Herod (23:15), the criminal on the cross (23:41) and the centurion (23:47). The same pattern runs through Paul's trials in Acts, where Roman officials find nothing deserving death (Acts 23:29; 25:25; 26:31–32). A defense to Rome: many scholars think Luke wanted readers in the empire to see that the Christian movement was no threat to order. A theological point: others stress that the innocent one dies for the guilty, as Isaiah's servant (22:37). Both can be true. See the deep dive on this chapter page.

p: Here "Judea" means the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included, as at 4:44 and Acts 10:37.
b: Luke sometimes uses Ioudaia for the Roman district around Jerusalem and sometimes for the whole Jewish homeland (1:5; 4:44; 7:17). The accusers' summary, starting from Galilee and reaching Jerusalem, echoes Peter's summary of Jesus' ministry in Acts: "They began in Galilee" (Acts 10:37), with the same Greek verb. What the accusers mean as a charge, Luke's readers hear as the gospel story.

p: A son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. He had beheaded John the Baptist.
b: Antipas was a "tetrarch," a minor ruler under Rome (3:1), and the one who had John the Baptist imprisoned and beheaded (3:19–20; 9:9). He wanted to see Jesus (9:9), and some Pharisees warned Jesus that Herod wanted to kill him; Jesus called him a fox (13:31–32). He was in Jerusalem for the festival, probably staying in the old Hasmonean palace. Sending a prisoner to the ruler of his home district was not required by Roman law, but it was a courtesy, and it gave Pilate a second opinion.

a: he was hoping to watch him do some sign
p: Herod had long wanted to see Jesus (9:9). He wants a show, and gets silence.
b: After hearing of Jesus' deeds, Herod wondered who this could be, since he had beheaded John, and he kept trying to see him (9:9). Jesus had refused to give a sign to those who demanded one (11:29). Before Herod he does no miracle and says nothing.

p: Before Herod, Jesus says nothing at all. Christians have heard Isaiah 53:7 in this silence.
b: Of Isaiah's servant it is said twice that "he did not open his mouth" (Isaiah 53:7), like a lamb led off to slaughter. In Mark and Matthew Jesus is silent before the high priest and Pilate; in Luke the full silence comes before Herod, the man who killed John. Acts quotes Isaiah 53:7 in the story of the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:32).

p: Exoutheneō means to count as nothing. Peter uses it in Acts of the rejected stone.
b: In Acts, Peter tells the council that Jesus is "the stone that you, the builders, treated as nothing" (Acts 4:11), changing the verb of Psalm 118:22 to this one. Jesus had said that the Son of Man must suffer much and be "counted as nothing" (Mark 9:12), the same verb in another spelling. Herod and his soldiers do exactly that.

p: Esthēs lampra is bright or splendid clothing. Was it a mock royal robe, or a white one?
b: Lampros means shining or splendid. Luke uses it for the clothes of the angel who appeared to Cornelius (Acts 10:30); James uses it for the fine clothes of the rich (James 2:2); compare the rich man who feasted "splendidly" (lamprōs, 16:19). Royal mockery: most take it as a costly robe to mock Jesus as a king, like the purple of Mark 15:17. White: some note that Roman candidates for office wore a whitened toga, and the Latin Vulgate renders it "white garment" (veste alba). Either way, the costume is a joke at the expense of a would-be king.

a: Herod and Pilate made friends with each other
p: Only Luke tells of the Herod hearing. Acts reads it through Psalm 2: "the rulers sit down together."
b: In Acts the church prays Psalm 2: "The kings of the earth station themselves, / the rulers sit down together" (Psalm 2:2), and names "Herod and Pontius Pilate" as those who gathered against Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). Philo tells of a quarrel when four Herodian princes, probably including Antipas, protested to Pilate over gilded shields he hung in Jerusalem (On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305), which may explain the old enmity. History: Harold Hoehner and others defend the scene as historical. Built from the psalm: some, such as Martin Dibelius, thought it grew out of Psalm 2. In the Gospel of Peter, a second-century text, Herod gives the order to crucify.

a: I have questioned him here in front of you
p: Anakrinas is a legal word for examining a prisoner. Pilate speaks as a judge who has done his duty.
b: Roman governors in the provinces tried cases themselves, questioning the accused and hearing the accusers, a procedure Roman historians call cognitio. Luke uses anakrinō for such examinations in Acts (Acts 4:9; 12:19; 24:8; 28:18). Pilate states the result like a magistrate: he has examined Jesus, and the charges fail.

a: So I will teach him a lesson
p: Paideusas, "having disciplined him," is a soft word for a beating, offered to satisfy the accusers.
b: Paideuō is the ordinary word for educating or disciplining a child. Here it means a flogging as a warning, a lighter punishment than the scourging before crucifixion. Roman officials used such beatings to settle disturbances without a death sentence (compare Acts 16:22–23; 22:24). Pilate offers it twice (23:16, 22). In Luke, unlike Mark 15:15 and John 19:1, Jesus is never actually flogged in the story.

p: The same cry is raised against Paul in Jerusalem (Acts 21:36; 22:22). Luke links the two trials.
b: Aire, "take away," means "kill him." Years later a Jerusalem crowd shouts "Away with him!" at Paul (Acts 21:36; 22:22). Luke tells Paul's arrest and hearings in ways that echo Jesus' passion: a plot in Jerusalem, a Roman governor, a Herod (Agrippa), and repeated findings of innocence.

a: an uprising that had happened in the city
p: Luke says twice that Barabbas was jailed for revolt and murder. The innocent man accused of revolt dies in his place.
b: Luke does not explain the release custom (see the variant at 23:17), but he stresses who Barabbas was (23:19, 25): a man actually guilty of the crime Jesus was falsely charged with, stirring up revolt. Mark speaks of "the uprising" as if it were well known (Mark 15:7). Peter puts the exchange sharply in Acts: "you asked to be granted a man who was a murderer" (Acts 3:14). On the name "Jesus Barabbas," see the variant at Matthew 27:16.

a: Jesus he handed over to what they wanted
p: Luke leaves the next "they" vague, and Acts blames the Jerusalem leaders. The passages were later misused against Jews.
b: In 23:26 "they" lead Jesus away, and Roman soldiers are not named until 23:36. Peter's speeches in Acts tell the people of Jerusalem, "you killed him" (Acts 2:23, 36; 3:13–15), while also blaming Herod, Pilate and the Gentiles (Acts 4:27) and saying they acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17). Hostile to Jews: Jack T. Sanders argued that Luke-Acts holds the Jewish people as a whole responsible. An intra-Jewish call: Jacob Jervell and others read it as Jews calling fellow Jews to repent, with thousands responding. Historically the crucifixion was a Roman act under Pilate. Christians long used these texts to blame all Jews of every age, a teaching the Catholic Church rejected in 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4). See the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: a man named Simon, from Cyrene
p: Cyrene, in Libya, had a large Jewish community. Mark names Simon's sons, Alexander and Rufus.
b: Cyrene was a Greek city on the coast of North Africa with many Jews (Acts 2:10), who had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9); men of Cyrene later preached to Greeks in Antioch (Acts 11:20; 13:1). Mark names Simon's sons as if readers knew them (Mark 15:21). In 1941 a burial cave in the Kidron Valley yielded ossuaries of a Jewish family from Cyrene, one inscribed "Alexander son of Simon" (published by Nahman Avigad in 1962); whether it was this family cannot be known.
r: Mark 15:21; Matthew 27:32; Acts 2:10; Acts 6:9; Acts 11:20; Acts 13:1

p: Only Luke says "behind Jesus." Simon becomes a picture of the disciple who takes up the cross and follows.
b: Jesus had said that anyone who wants to come after him must take up his cross every day and follow him (9:23), and that whoever does not carry his own cross and come after him cannot be his disciple (14:27). Mark and Matthew say Simon was made to carry the cross; Luke adds that he carried it "behind Jesus." Simon does what the Twelve, absent from the scene, should have done.

a: who beat their breasts and sang laments for him
p: Mourning the dead with chest-beating and sung laments was women's work in Israel and across the Mediterranean.
b: Professional and family mourners, mostly women, wailed for the dead (Jeremiah 9:17–20; 2 Chronicles 35:25). Mourning for a condemned criminal could be dangerous. These women of Jerusalem, distinct from the women of Galilee (23:49, 55), show public grief. Zechariah foresaw Jerusalem mourning for "the one they have pierced" (Zechariah 12:10–14), a passage John applies to the cross (John 19:37).

p: Jesus' last prophecy before the cross is a lament for Jerusalem, like 13:34–35, 19:41–44 and 21:20–24.
b: Luke has Jesus grieve over Jerusalem four times: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem" (13:34–35), his weeping as he saw the city (19:41–44), the armies surrounding it (21:20–24), and here. The words look ahead to the siege of AD 70, when Josephus says famine was so terrible that mothers lost their children (Jewish War 6.201–213). The tone is grief, not gloating: the women weep for Jesus, and he weeps for them. Many scholars think Luke's wording reflects the city's fall, which had happened by the time he wrote.

p: In Israel childlessness was grief and children a blessing. In the coming days the opposite will be said.
b: Elizabeth's barrenness had been her disgrace (1:25), and a woman had called out a blessing on the womb that carried Jesus (11:27). Jesus had warned of woe for pregnant and nursing women in the days of the city's fall (21:23). Now he says that in the coming disaster the childless will be called happy, since they will not see their children suffer. Isaiah had used the image the other way, calling the barren woman to sing because her children would be many (Isaiah 54:1).

p: Jesus quotes Hosea 10:8. Revelation 6:16 uses the same cry for the day of God's anger.
b: Hosea spoke of Samaria's judgment, when people would beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them (Hosea 10:8). In Revelation, people of every rank call to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us! Hide us" (Revelation 6:16). In each case the cry is a wish to die rather than face what is coming.

a: If this is what they do to green wood
p: A proverb: if green, living wood burns like this, how much more the dry? Who are "they"?
b: Green wood is hard to burn; dry wood catches at once. Rome and Jerusalem: if the Romans do this to an innocent man, what will they do to a rebellious city? The people and their leaders: if Jerusalem treats its Messiah this way, what will become of it later? God and sinners: if God allows the innocent one to suffer so, what will the guilty face? Ezekiel pictures God's fire burning every green tree and every dry tree (Ezekiel 20:47). Many readers combine the first and third readings.

p: The Greek can be read "two other criminals," as if Jesus were one too. Luke's wording fulfills 22:37.
b: Heteroi kakourgoi duo literally reads "other evildoers, two." Read strictly it numbers Jesus among the criminals, which is what Isaiah 53:12 foretold and Jesus quoted: "he was counted with the lawless" (22:37). The Plain keeps the sense without suggesting that Luke thinks Jesus guilty, since Luke's whole account insists he was not. Luke calls the two kakourgoi, "evildoers"; Mark and Matthew call them lēstai, "bandits" (Mark 15:27).

p: Luke gives only the Greek name, Kranion. The Aramaic is Golgotha; the Latin, Calvaria, gives "Calvary."
b: Mark and Matthew give the Aramaic name Golgotha and translate it "Skull Place" (Mark 15:22). Luke, writing for Greek readers, gives only Kranion, "Skull." The Latin Vulgate rendered it Calvaria, from which the King James Version took "Calvary" in this verse. The name may come from the shape of a rocky knoll or from executions there; a later legend said Adam's skull was buried beneath it.

p: The soldiers who nailed him? The leaders? The people? Readers have answered each way.
b: The soldiers, who did not know whom they were crucifying: the nearest group in the scene. The leaders and people of Jerusalem, who acted "in ignorance," as Peter says in Acts 3:17. All who had a hand in it, Jew and Gentile alike. Jesus had taught, "Pray for the ones who abuse you" (6:28), and Stephen prays the same way as he dies: "Lord, do not count this sin against them!" (Acts 7:60). The words are missing from some early manuscripts; see the variant on this verse.

a: They shared out his clothes by throwing lots
p: The soldiers act out Psalm 22: "over my clothing they throw lots."
b: Psalm 22, the prayer of a righteous sufferer, says: "They hand out my clothes among them, / and over my clothing they throw lots" (Psalm 22:18). All four Gospels tell this detail; John quotes the psalm outright (John 19:24). Luke's Greek is close to Matthew 27:35 (Luke diamerizomenoi ... ebalon klērous, Matthew diemerisanto ... ballontes klēron), and the Plain renders both alike. In Roman practice the executioners kept the clothes of the crucified.

p: Luke separates the people, who watch, from the rulers, who sneer. Psalm 22 lies behind both.
b: In Mark and Matthew the passers-by mock Jesus (Mark 15:29). Luke says "the people stood by, watching" and gives the mockery to "the rulers." Psalm 22:7 says: "All who see me make fun of me; / they sneer with their lips and shake their heads" (Psalm 22:7). In the Greek of that verse "all who watch me" sneer, and Luke divides the line: the people watch (theōrōn), the rulers "turned up their noses" (ekmyktērizō, "sneer"). The people's watching ends in grief (23:48).

p: The rulers mock him with the title the voice from the cloud gave him: "my Son, the Chosen One" (9:35).
b: At the transfiguration the voice said, "This is my Son, the Chosen One" (9:35). Isaiah's servant is God's chosen (Isaiah 42:1), and in the Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 37–71, which the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts as Scripture) "the Chosen One" is a heavenly judge also called the Son of Man and the Anointed. The mockers use the true titles without knowing it. Peter had called Jesus "God's Messiah" (9:20), the same phrase used here.
orig: ὁ χριστὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἐκλεκτός (ho christos tou theou, ho eklektos)

p: Cheap sour wine was soldiers' drink. Psalm 69 says, "when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar."
b: Oxos was a sharp, watered wine that soldiers and laborers drank. In Mark and Matthew someone offers it near the end; in Luke the soldiers hold it out as part of their mockery. Psalm 69 says: "they made me drink vinegar" (Psalm 69:21), and the Greek Old Testament uses oxos there.

a: "The King of the Jews, this man."
p: Each Gospel gives the notice in slightly different words. Luke's order is "The King of the Jews, this one."
b: Mark: "The King of the Jews" (Mark 15:26). Matthew: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews" (Matthew 27:37). John: "Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews," in three languages (John 19:19–20). Luke puts "this man" last, which can sound like a sneer: this is the King of the Jews. The differences show that the Gospels remember the substance, the charge of claiming kingship, rather than an exact text.

a: One of the criminals hanging there
p: Mark and Matthew say both men crucified with Jesus insulted him. Luke says one did, and the other defended him.
b: Mark 15:32 and Matthew 27:44 say the men crucified with him threw insults at him. A figure of speech: Augustine suggested Matthew and Mark used the plural loosely for one person (Harmony of the Gospels 3.16). A change of heart: others suggest both mocked at first and one changed. Luke's own source: many scholars think Luke had a separate tradition. "Hanging" recalls the Law's words about a man hanged on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), which Peter uses of Jesus in Acts 5:30 and 10:39.
r: Mark 15:32; Matthew 27:44; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39; Galatians 3:13

p: Later tradition named him Dismas. The Gospels give no name.
b: Luke's word kakourgos means "evildoer"; Christian tradition calls him the penitent or good thief. The Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus (an early Christian work, probably fourth century, in no church's Bible), names him Dysmas and the other Gestas. The Catholic calendar remembered "Saint Dismas" on March 25, and Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches honor him in the hymns of Holy Week. His question is "Don't you even (oude) fear God?": the word "even" goes with fearing God.

a: has done nothing out of place
p: Atopon means "out of place, improper": a mild word. Not even a small wrong.
b: The criminal does not only say Jesus is not a rebel; he says Jesus has done nothing improper at all. Luke uses atopos again when Paul's accusers can find "nothing wrong" (Acts 25:5) and when the islanders expect Paul to swell up (Acts 28:6). The criminal is one more witness to Jesus' innocence (see the note at 23:4), and he also admits his own guilt, the posture Luke calls repentance.

p: The man calls him simply "Jesus." His prayer has become one of the church's most used.
b: In Luke people address Jesus as "Master," "Teacher," "Lord," "Son of David" or "Jesus, Son of God" (8:28); this man alone calls him by his bare name. "Remember me" is the cry of the Psalms (Psalm 106:4) and of Joseph to the cupbearer (Genesis 40:14). In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy the prayer before communion says, "like the thief I confess you: Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom," and the Beatitudes are sung with the same refrain. The short chant "Jesus, remember me" from the Taizé community is sung across the churches.

p: Greek manuscripts had little punctuation. Is it "I tell you today, you will be" or "today you will be"?
b: "Today you will be with me": almost all translations and commentators read it this way. Jesus' formula "Amen, I tell you" never adds "today" anywhere else, and "today" is one of Luke's key words for salvation arriving (2:11; 4:21; 19:5, 9). "I tell you today, you will be with me": Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses and other Christians who hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection put the comma after "today": Jesus is speaking solemnly on this day about the future. The question of where the dead are before the resurrection is treated on the card at 16:19–31.

p: A Persian word for a walled garden. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Eden; Jews, for the place of the righteous dead.
b: Paradeisos came from Persian into Greek as a word for a royal park. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden in Eden (Genesis 2:8). Jewish writings of Jesus' time speak of paradise as the place where the righteous wait (1 Enoch 60:8; 61:12), and Paul says he was caught up into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:4). Revelation promises "the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7). The garden lost at the beginning is promised to a dying criminal.

p: From noon until three. Amos had spoken of a day when God would make the sun go down at noon.
b: Luke follows Mark's hours (Mark 15:33). Amos warned that on that day God would make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9), and darkness was the ninth plague in Egypt (Exodus 10:21–23). The deep dive at Mark 15 compares the Gospels' hours.

p: Luke's verb is the word for an eclipse. But a solar eclipse cannot happen at Passover, when the moon is full.
b: Tou hēliou eklipontos literally means "the sun having failed," and ekleipsis was the Greek word for an eclipse. At Passover the moon is full and so cannot pass in front of the sun. Julius Africanus, about AD 221, already rejected a writer named Thallus for calling the darkness an eclipse (Chronography, in later quotations). Not an eclipse: Luke may simply mean that the sun gave out, by cloud, dust storm or a sign from God. A copyist's fix: many later manuscripts read "the sun was darkened," perhaps to avoid the problem; see the variant. The same verb is used of Peter's faith in 22:32.

a: the sanctuary curtain was torn down the middle
t: The torn curtain, before his death
p: Mark and Matthew tell of the curtain after Jesus dies. Luke tells it before, with the darkness.
b: Luke joins the torn curtain to the failing sun as signs of judgment and change. Readers have seen in it the end of the old order of the temple, the opening of God's presence to all (Hebrews 10:19–20), or a sign of mourning, like tearing one's clothes. Yet in Luke the disciples go on worshiping in the temple (24:53; Acts 2:46; 3:1). The deep dives at Mark 15 and Matthew 27 set out the readings; the Plain keeps Mark's wording "the sanctuary curtain was torn."

a: Father, into your hands I place my spirit
p: Jesus' last words in Luke come from Psalm 31:5, a prayer that Jews have used as a bedtime prayer.
b: Psalm 31 says: "Into your hand I place my spirit. / You have ransomed me, LORD, faithful God" (Psalm 31:5). Jesus adds "Father." Where Mark and Matthew give the cry of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?", Luke gives this prayer of trust. Jewish tradition uses the psalm verse at bedtime, and the hymn "Adon Olam" ends: "Into his hand I commit my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake." Stephen dies with a similar prayer, addressed to Jesus: "Lord Jesus, welcome my spirit" (Acts 7:59).
r: Psalm 31:5; 2:49; Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:46; John 19:30; Acts 7:59; 1 Peter 4:19

p: Dikaios means both "innocent" and "righteous." Mark and Matthew's centurion says "God's Son."
b: Many translations read "innocent," which fits Luke's chain of verdicts (see the note at 23:4). The Plain keeps "righteous," because Luke uses the word as a title: in Acts Jesus is the "Holy and Righteous One" (Acts 3:14) and "the Righteous One" (Acts 7:52; 22:14), echoing Isaiah's "righteous one, my servant" (Isaiah 53:11). The Wisdom of Solomon has the ungodly test a righteous man to see whether the righteous man is God's son (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18), joining the two confessions. Mark's centurion says, "This man really was God's Son!" (Mark 15:39).
r: Mark 15:39; Matthew 27:54; Acts 3:14; Acts 7:52; Acts 22:14; Isaiah 53:11; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20

t: Glory to God from a Roman
p: Throughout Luke, people who see God's work "give glory to God." Now a Gentile soldier does, at a death.
b: Shepherds (2:20), a healed paralytic (5:25), the crowd at Nain (7:16), the bent woman (13:13), the Samaritan healed of skin disease (17:15) and the blind man (18:43) all give glory to God. The centurion does so at the death of Jesus. Luke tells of another God-fearing centurion, Cornelius, who becomes the first Gentile believer in Acts (Acts 10).

a: they went back beating their chests
p: Only Luke tells of the crowds' sorrow. Beating the chest is a sign of grief and repentance.
b: The tax collector in the temple kept striking his chest and saying, "God, be gracious to me, the sinner" (18:13). The crowds who had come to watch now go home in grief. Luke seems to prepare for Pentecost, when Peter's words "pierced their hearts" and three thousand repented (Acts 2:37–41). Luke shows the people of Jerusalem moved, not hardened.

p: The psalms of suffering say friends and relatives stand far off. Luke uses the same words.
b: Psalm 38 says: "My friends and companions keep their distance from the blow that struck me; / my relatives stay a long way off" (Psalm 38:11), and Psalm 88 complains, "You have put distance between me and those who know me" (Psalm 88:8). In the Greek Old Testament Psalm 87 (88) uses "those who know me" (tous gnōstous mou), the word Luke uses here, "all who knew him." Only Luke places Jesus' acquaintances, perhaps including the Eleven, at the cross.

a: the women who had followed along with him from Galilee
p: The same women who supported Jesus in Galilee (8:1–3) see his death, his burial and the empty tomb.
b: Luke named some of them at 8:2–3: Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, "and many others, who supported them from their own means." He will name them again at the tomb (24:10). They are the link between the cross, the burial and the resurrection: they see where the body is laid (23:55), so they do not go to the wrong tomb. In the ancient world women's testimony counted for little (see the note at 24:10), which makes their place in the story all the more striking.

t: Joseph, a member of the council
p: Joseph sat on the Sanhedrin. Luke stresses that he had not agreed with its decision.
b: Bouleutēs means a council member; Mark calls him "a council member of high standing" (Mark 15:43). Luke adds that he was "good and righteous" and had not voted with the others, a reminder that the council was not of one mind (compare Nicodemus, John 7:50–51; Gamaliel, Acts 5:34–39). Luke says the council's decision was not unanimous, which fits his care to separate individuals from groups.

a: he was looking for the kingdom of God
p: Joseph is like Simeon and Anna at the start: a devout Jew looking for God to act.
b: Luke uses the same verb, prosdechomai, "wait for, look for," of Simeon, who was looking forward to the comforting of Israel (2:25), and of those to whom Anna spoke, who were looking for Jerusalem to be redeemed (2:38). The Plain follows Mark 15:43 here with "looking for," as at 2:38. The Gospel opens and closes with faithful Jews looking for God's promises. See the spec box on this chapter page.

a: where nobody had been laid yet
p: Like the colt no one had ridden (19:30), the tomb is new: fit for a king, and unmixed with other remains.
b: Things set apart for holy use were often things never used before: a red heifer that had never borne a yoke (Numbers 19:2), new carts for the ark (1 Samuel 6:7). Jesus entered Jerusalem on a colt no one had ever ridden (19:30), and he is laid in a tomb no one has used. A new tomb also meant that no one could mistake his body for another's. John adds that the tomb was in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41).

a: the Sabbath was beginning to dawn
t: "The Sabbath was dawning" in the evening
p: Epephōsken means "was dawning," though the Sabbath began at sunset. Why?
b: The Jewish day begins at evening (Leviticus 23:32), so the Sabbath began on Friday at sunset. Luke's verb, "was beginning to shine," may simply mean "was beginning," as in Matthew 28:1. Some suggest it refers to the lighting of the Sabbath lamps, or to the first evening star. Either way the burial had to be finished before dark, both because of the Sabbath and because the Law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23).

a: as the commandment says, they kept the Sabbath rest
p: Even with the body of Jesus waiting, the women keep the Sabbath. Luke shows Jesus' followers as Torah-observant Jews.
b: The commandment says of the seventh day: "Do no work on it" (Exodus 20:10). The women wait until Sunday to finish the burial rites. Luke began his Gospel with families who did everything "according to the Law" (2:22–24, 39) and ends the passion the same way. In Acts the first believers still keep the temple hours and the Law (Acts 3:1; 21:20–26). Luke does not show Jesus' death ending his followers' Jewish life.

a: On the first day of the week
p: The Greek says "on one of the Sabbaths," a Hebrew way of saying "on day one of the week": Sunday.
b: Tē mia tōn sabbatōn uses "Sabbaths" for the week and "one" for "first," following Hebrew usage. All four Gospels date the empty tomb to this day (Mark 16:2; Matthew 28:1; John 20:1). Christians soon gathered on it: Paul's churches set money aside on the first day of the week (1 Corinthians 16:2), and in Acts the believers at Troas gather on the first day of the week to break bread (Acts 20:7). Revelation calls it "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10).
orig: τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων (tē mia tōn sabbatōn)
r: Mark 16:2; Matthew 28:1; John 20:1; Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10

p: Luke's "two men" link the tomb, the transfiguration and the ascension. Mark has one young man; Matthew one angel.
b: At the transfiguration "two men," Moses and Elijah, spoke with Jesus about his departure (9:30–31). At the ascension "two men in white clothing" stand beside the disciples (Acts 1:10). The Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Mark has a young man in a white robe (Mark 16:5), Matthew an angel of the Lord (Matthew 28:2–5), John two angels (John 20:12). Luke calls them men here and later says the women saw angels (24:23).

p: The Greek is singular, "the living one." Revelation calls the risen Jesus "the Living One."
b: Ton zōnta is "the one who is living," not "the living" in general. Revelation has the risen Christ say: "the one who lives. I died, and look, I am alive forever and ever!" (Revelation 1:18). In the Old Testament "the living God" sets Israel's God apart from dead idols; the question puts Jesus in that light, and also has a touch of irony: why look in a graveyard for someone alive?

a: Remember how he spoke to you
p: In Mark the women are told Jesus is going ahead to Galilee. In Luke they are told to remember what he said in Galilee.
b: Mark 16:7 and Matthew 28:7 point the disciples to Galilee, where Matthew tells of the final meeting. Luke turns the Galilee word into a memory and keeps every appearance in or near Jerusalem, from which the good news will go to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:4, 8). Harmonizers say Luke simply chose the Jerusalem appearances, while John 21 and Matthew 28 tell of Galilee. Many critical scholars see Luke reshaping the tradition to fit his plan, in which Jerusalem is the center. The women are told to remember Jesus' own predictions (9:22, 44; 18:31–33), and they do (24:8): faith begins with remembering his words.

p: Dei, "it is necessary," marks God's plan. It comes three times in this chapter (24:7, 26, 44).
b: Luke uses dei more than any other Gospel writer. Jesus "must" be at his Father's (2:49), "must" preach the kingdom (4:43), "must" suffer (9:22; 17:25), "must" go on to Jerusalem (13:33). In chapter 24 the word returns three times (24:7, 26, 44). It means that the cross was not an accident, but the path God had marked out and the Scriptures had foretold.

a: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James
p: Luke names three women, and the rest. Women's witness counted for little in law, yet the Gospels name them first.
b: Mary Magdalene and Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, were named among the women who supported Jesus (8:2–3); Mary the mother of James is named in Mark 16:1. Josephus says that in Jewish law "the testimony of women" is not accepted, "because of the lightness and boldness of their sex" (Jewish Antiquities 4.219), and pagan critics such as Celsus later mocked a faith resting on a "hysterical woman" (Origen, Against Celsus 2.55). Many historians argue that no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses. Richard Bauckham argues that the names point to the eyewitnesses behind the account.

p: Lēros is idle talk, nonsense; medical writers used it of the raving of fever. The apostles do not believe.
b: The word appears only here in the New Testament. Luke does not hide the apostles' unbelief: they dismiss the women, and even after Jesus appears they are still "disbelieving for joy" (24:41). The Longer Ending of Mark says the same (Mark 16:11). The doubts of the first witnesses became part of the church's case: the apostles had to be convinced.

p: John 20:3–10 tells the same visit, with the beloved disciple too, in nearly the same Greek.
b: John says Peter and "the other disciple" ran to the tomb; the other disciple "bent down to peer in and saw the linen wrappings lying there" (John 20:5), and afterward "the disciples went off home again" (John 20:10). Luke's verse has the same rare words: "bending down," "the linen wrappings," "went off home." Luke later has Cleopas say that "some of our people" went to the tomb (24:24), plural, which fits John's two runners. The verse is missing from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts; see the variant on this verse and the deep dive.

p: Four places claim the name. None fits every detail of Luke's distance.
b: Emmaus-Nicopolis (modern Imwas), a well-known town of the Maccabean wars (1 Maccabees 3:40), honored as the site by Eusebius and Jerome; but it lies about 160 stadia (18 miles) away, too far to walk there and back in an evening, unless one reads the variant "a hundred and sixty stadia." El-Qubeibeh, about sixty stadia away, honored since the Crusades. Abu Ghosh, about sixty stadia, also venerated by Crusaders. Motza, which Josephus calls Emmaus and places thirty stadia from Jerusalem, where Vespasian settled veterans after the war (Jewish War 7.217). Many scholars favor Motza or Nicopolis.

t: Why did they not recognize him?
p: Luke says their eyes "were held." By God, or by their own grief and expectations?
b: By God: the passive voice is often a reverent way of saying God did it, and the opening of their eyes at 24:31 is also passive. Jesus' predictions had been "hidden" from the disciples (9:45; 18:34). By themselves: others think grief and dashed hopes kept them from seeing what they did not expect. A changed body: some point to the risen Jesus' appearance "in a different form" (Mark 16:12) and to Mary Magdalene's failure to recognize him (John 20:14). Ancient stories often turn on a late recognition, but Luke ties this one to the Scriptures and the bread.

p: Early tradition says Clopas was Joseph's brother. If Cleopas is the same man, the other traveler may have been his wife.
b: The second-century writer Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, says Clopas was the brother of Joseph and the father of Symeon, who led the Jerusalem church after James (Church History 3.11). John 19:25 names "Mary of Clopas" at the cross. Cleopas (a Greek name) and Clopas (a Semitic one) may be the same man, as Richard Bauckham argues, and some suggest that the unnamed companion was his wife Mary. Luke does not say. The traveler's name may mean he was known to Luke's first readers.

a: a prophet, a man of power in what he did and what he said
p: Stephen says the same of Moses in Acts 7:22. Luke presents Jesus as the prophet like Moses.
b: In Acts Stephen says Moses "had power in his words and in his actions" (Acts 7:22). Moses promised that God would raise up "a prophet like me" (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Peter and Stephen apply the promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37). The travelers are right that Jesus was a prophet; they do not yet see that, like Moses, he was rejected before he rescued his people (Acts 7:35).

a: the man who would redeem Israel
p: The travelers' hope is the hope of Zechariah, Anna and the psalms: God would set Israel free.
b: Lytroō means to ransom or set free. Zechariah praised God for bringing redemption to his people (1:68), and Anna spoke to those waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:38). Many Jews hoped for a Messiah who would free Israel from Rome (Psalms of Solomon 17). The disciples' question in Acts 1:6 shows the same hope. Luke does not say the hope was wrong; he says it was fulfilled in a way they had not foreseen, through suffering (24:26).
r: 1:68; 2:38; 21:28; Acts 1:6; Acts 7:35; Titus 2:14; Psalms of Solomon 17:21–25

p: "On the third day" was already part of the church's earliest creed, "according to the Scriptures."
b: Paul hands on the confession that Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4). Christians have pointed to Hosea 6:2, where Israel says that on the third day God will raise us up, and to Jonah's three days in the fish (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:40). Jesus had predicted rising on the third day (9:22; 18:33).

a: The Messiah had to suffer all this
p: Most Jews of the time did not expect a Messiah who would be killed. Later rabbis spoke of a dying Messiah son of Joseph.
b: Jewish hopes varied, but most pictured a victorious king of David's line (Psalms of Solomon 17). Jewish interpreters have usually read Isaiah 52:13–53:12 of Israel, a prophet or a righteous remnant. The Babylonian Talmud, much later, speaks of a Messiah son of Joseph who is killed (Sukkah 52a), which shows that the idea of a dying Messiah was not unthinkable in Judaism, though it is not the same as the Christian claim. Jesus' answer is that the Scriptures read as a whole show the path through suffering to glory. See the note at Acts 3:18.
r: Isaiah 52:13–53:12; Psalm 22; Zechariah 12:10; Acts 3:18; Acts 17:3; Acts 26:22–23; 1 Peter 1:10–11

a: he explained to them the things about himself in all the Scriptures
p: Luke does not list them. The rest of the New Testament shows which passages the first Christians read this way.
b: Diermēneusen, "he interpreted," is the root of "hermeneutics." Luke's readers can fill in the lesson from Acts: Psalm 2, Psalm 16, Psalm 110, Psalm 118, Isaiah 53, Deuteronomy 18 and Joel 2. C. H. Dodd argued that the first Christians read whole sections of the Old Testament, not proof texts alone, as pointing to Christ. Jewish readers have answered that these passages have their own meaning in Israel's history. Christian tradition also reads figures such as Adam, Isaac, Moses and David as types, patterns that point ahead (see the topic on typology).

p: The two invite a stranger in. At the table he takes the host's part.
b: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in Israel; Abraham's guests turned out to be messengers of God (Genesis 18), and Hebrews says some have entertained angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2). The two press the stranger to stay, as Lydia later "pressed" Paul with the same rare verb (Acts 16:15). Once inside, the guest breaks the bread, which was the host's role. In Luke, Jesus is again and again the guest who becomes the host (5:29; 7:36; 19:5–7).

a: he took the bread and said the blessing
p: The four actions, took, blessed, broke, gave, repeat the feeding of the 5,000 and the Last Supper.
b: At the feeding Jesus took the loaves, blessed them, broke them and gave them (9:16), and at the supper he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it (22:19). A Eucharist: many readers in every tradition see the Emmaus meal as the first Lord's Supper of the risen church, and Luke's summary, "in the breaking of the bread" (24:35), is the phrase Acts uses for the church's gatherings (Acts 2:42). An ordinary meal: others note that the two were not at the Last Supper and that the blessing and breaking were how any Jewish host began a meal; what matters is that Jesus is known at table, as he always was.

p: Genesis 3:7 says, after the first meal, "The eyes of the two of them were opened." Luke's Greek is close.
b: The Greek Old Testament of Genesis 3:7 says diēnoichthēsan hoi ophthalmoi, "their eyes were opened," the same words Luke uses here. In Eden two people eat and their eyes are opened to shame; at Emmaus two people eat and their eyes are opened to the risen Lord. Several interpreters have drawn the comparison. Luke uses the verb three times in this chapter: eyes opened (24:31), Scriptures opened (24:32), minds opened (24:45). Then Jesus vanishes: from now on he will be known in the word and the bread.

p: Psalm 39 says, "My heart was burning inside me." Jeremiah says God's word was like fire in his bones.
b: Psalm 39:3 says: "My heart was burning inside me," and Jeremiah says the LORD's word was like a burning fire shut up in his bones (Jeremiah 20:9). The travelers' hearts "burned" as Jesus opened the Scriptures. Christian writers have used the image ever since; John Wesley wrote in 1738 that at a meeting in Aldersgate Street he "felt my heart strangely warmed" as someone read Luther's preface to Romans. A few manuscripts read differently here; see the variant.

p: Paul lists it first, before the Twelve. The Gospels never tell the scene.
b: Paul's early list of witnesses begins with Cephas, Peter's Aramaic name, then the Twelve (1 Corinthians 15:5). Luke mentions it only in passing, in the mouth of the Eleven. No Gospel narrates it. Jesus had prayed that Peter's faith would not fail and that, once turned around, he would strengthen his brothers (22:32); now the one who denied him is the first apostle to see him. The verb ōphthē, "was seen, appeared," is the word used for God's appearances to Abraham and Moses in the Greek Old Testament.

a: in the breaking of the bread
p: Acts uses the same phrase for the church's meals: "to the breaking of the bread and to the prayers."
