b: The first believers "held steadily ... to the breaking of the bread and to the prayers" (Acts 2:42). Luke's readers, who met to break bread on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7), would hear the Emmaus story as their own: the risen Lord is known when the Scriptures are opened and the bread is broken. Christian worship in many traditions still has those two parts, word and table.

p: Pneuma here means a ghost, a spirit of the dead. Jesus answers that a spirit has no flesh and bones.
b: Many people in the ancient world believed the dead could appear as shades or phantoms. The disciples assume the figure is a spirit (compare the "ghost" on the water, Mark 6:49, where the word is phantasma). In Acts the Pharisees say perhaps a spirit or an angel spoke to Paul (Acts 23:8–9). Luke answers the idea directly in the verses that follow.

a: a spirit has no flesh and bones
p: Luke stresses a bodily resurrection. Christians read this beside Paul's "spiritual body."
b: Jesus invites them to see the hands and feet (the nail wounds, though Luke does not say so) and to "feel" him, the word used in 1 John 1:1 for what the writer's hands have handled. About AD 110 Ignatius of Antioch quotes a saying of the risen Jesus: "Take hold, handle me and see that I am not a bodiless demon" (To the Smyrnaeans 3.2). Bodily continuity: most Christians, and scholars such as N. T. Wright, read Luke and Paul together: the same body, transformed (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Contrast: some critical scholars think Luke stresses flesh to answer docetists, who said Christ only seemed to have a body, and that Paul's "spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44, 50) reflects an earlier view. Dale Allison weighs both sides.

a: Their joy was so great that they still could not believe it
p: Luke says they disbelieved "from joy." Rhoda leaves Peter at the gate for the same reason (Acts 12:14).
b: The Greek says they were disbelieving apo tēs charas, "from the joy." Luke is kind to the disciples here, as at 22:45, where they slept "from grief." In Acts the servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed to hear Peter's voice that she leaves him knocking at the gate (Acts 12:14). Joy is one of Luke's great themes, from the angel's "good news of a great joy" (2:10) to the last verse (24:52).

p: Eating shows he is no spirit. In Tobit the angel says he only seemed to eat. Peter says, "We shared meals with him."
b: In the book of Tobit (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) the angel Raphael says at his departure, "I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision" (Tobit 12:19). Jesus eats in front of them, so that they will not think the same of him. Peter later says the witnesses were the ones who "shared meals with him, eating and drinking, after he rose from among the dead" (Acts 10:41). John too has the risen Jesus serve grilled fish by the lake (John 21:9–13).

a: the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms
p: The three parts of the Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets, and the Writings, which begin with the Psalms.
b: The Hebrew Bible is arranged in three parts: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi'im) and the Writings (Ketuvim), which in most lists begin with Psalms. The Greek prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC) speaks of the Law, the Prophets and the other books that followed them, and a Dead Sea Scroll known as 4QMMT speaks of "the book of Moses, the books of the prophets and David." Luke 24:44 is the New Testament's clearest witness to a three-part Scripture. Whether the third part was closed in Jesus' day, and which books it held, is debated; see the "Where Christians differ" card on this chapter page and the topic on the canon.

a: Then he opened up their minds
p: The same verb as 24:31 and 24:32: first their eyes, then the Scriptures, now their minds.
b: Dianoigō means to open fully. In Acts the Lord "opened" Lydia's heart to pay attention to Paul (Acts 16:14), and Paul "opened" the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica (Acts 17:3). Luke teaches that understanding the Scriptures as speaking of Christ is a gift of the risen Lord, not only a matter of study.

a: on the third day he would rise from among the dead
p: Christians pointed to Psalm 16 and Hosea 6:2. Acts quotes Psalm 16: "you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit."
b: Jesus gives no chapter and verse. In Acts Peter and Paul argue from Psalm 16: "you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit" (Psalm 16:10), which the Greek Old Testament renders "see decay" (Acts 2:27; 13:35). For the third day, Christians cited Hosea 6:2 and the sign of Jonah. The phrase "from among the dead" is the usual New Testament way of speaking of resurrection out of the realm of the dead.

t: To all the nations, starting from Jerusalem
p: Isaiah's servant is "a light to the nations." Acts follows it: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth.
b: Isaiah says of God's servant: "I will give you as a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6), a verse Paul quotes in Acts 13:47. Simeon had sung of a light to bring revelation to the nations (2:32). The Greek participle "starting" is plural, pointing to the disciples: "you, starting from Jerusalem." Acts 1:8 sets out the route, and the book ends in Rome. Luke's Gospel ends where his second volume begins.

a: You are the witnesses to all this
p: Martyres, witnesses. Because so many witnesses died for their testimony, the word became English "martyr."
b: In Acts, being "witnesses" of the resurrection is the apostles' task (Acts 1:8, 22; 2:32; 3:15; 10:39–41). Stephen is called Jesus' "witness" when his blood is shed (Acts 22:20), and in Revelation the word is already moving toward the meaning "one who dies for the faith" (Revelation 2:13; 17:6). By the second century martys meant martyr.

p: The promise is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; 2:33).
b: Jesus does not name the gift here, but Acts does: "wait for the Father's promise" (Acts 1:4), and at Pentecost Peter says, "The Father promised the Holy Spirit, and Jesus has received that promise from him" (Acts 2:33). The prophets had foretold it: "until a spirit from on high is poured out on us" (Isaiah 32:15); Joel 2:28.

a: dressed in power from on high
p: The Spirit is pictured as clothing. Isaiah speaks of a spirit "from on high," and Elisha took up Elijah's cloak.
b: To be "clothed" with something is a Bible image for being filled and marked by it: the Spirit "clothed" Gideon (Judges 6:34, literally), and Paul speaks of putting on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Isaiah 32:15 speaks of a spirit "from on high." Many readers recall Elisha, who saw Elijah taken up and picked up his cloak, receiving a double share of his spirit (2 Kings 2:9–15); Jesus too will be taken up, and his followers will receive his Spirit. Gabriel told Mary that the power of the Most High would overshadow her (1:35).

a: He lifted his hands and blessed them
p: Aaron "lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them." A Gospel that began with a silent priest ends in blessing.
b: Leviticus 9:22 says: "Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them." Sirach describes the high priest Simon coming out of the sanctuary and lifting his hands to bless the people (Sirach 50:20–21). Luke's Gospel began with the priest Zechariah coming out of the sanctuary unable to speak the blessing the people waited for (1:21–22). It ends with Jesus lifting his hands and blessing his people. Many commentators note the frame; Hebrews calls Jesus a high priest who has gone into heaven (Hebrews 4:14).

t: Bethany and the Mount of Olives
p: Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives. Acts 1:12 says they returned from the Mount of Olives.
b: Luke's Gospel says Jesus led them out toward Bethany; Acts says they came back from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:12). Bethany was a village on the far side of that hill, about two miles from Jerusalem (John 11:18), and Jesus had stayed nearby (19:29; 21:37). The two accounts agree on the place. See the note at Acts 1:12.

p: Read alone, Luke 24 seems to put the ascension on Easter day; Acts 1:3 says forty days later. One author wrote both.
b: Luke 24 moves from the empty tomb (24:1) to Emmaus (24:13), the return that night (24:33), the appearance (24:36) and the departure (24:50) without a mark of time. Acts says Jesus appeared over forty days (Acts 1:3). Compression: the Gospel summarizes; "then" in 24:44 and 24:50 need not mean the same night. Two purposes: the Gospel closes Jesus' story with a blessing; Acts opens the church's story with a commission. Different traditions: some critical scholars think Luke learned a fuller account after writing the Gospel. The words "and was being carried up into heaven" are missing from some manuscripts; see the variant on this verse and the topic on the ascension. Heaven or sky: the same Greek, eis ton ouranon, is "into heaven" here and "into the sky" at Acts 1:10–11, where the two men ask why the apostles stand staring up; the word means both, and the note at Acts 1:11 says so.

p: The verb means to bow down, and also to worship. In Luke only God is to be worshiped (4:8). Now they bow to Jesus.
b: Proskyneō means to bow down to the ground and also to worship. In the testing in the wilderness Jesus told the devil that one must bow down to God alone (4:8, quoting Deuteronomy 6:13). This is the first time in Luke's Gospel that anyone bows down before Jesus. Luke does not comment; he lets the reader draw the conclusion. On Christian views of worshiping Jesus, see the card at Matthew 28:9.

a: in the temple all the time
p: Luke's Gospel begins and ends in the temple. The first believers are Jews praising Israel's God in his house.
b: The story opened with Zechariah burning incense in the sanctuary (1:8–10), and Mary and Joseph brought the child Jesus there (2:22–38, 41–51). It closes with the disciples "blessing God" in the temple, and Acts begins with them there daily (Acts 2:46; 3:1). For Luke, the followers of Jesus did not leave Israel or its worship; they were Israel's faithful remnant, waiting in Jerusalem for the promised Spirit.
